Importunate Widow
im-POR-choo-nit WID-oh
n. phrase (parable of Luke 18:1–8; the persistent widow who pressed an unjust judge until he granted her justice — a model of persistent, faith-sustained prayer)
Importunate from Latin importunus (troublesome, pressing, persistent without regard to convenience), from in- + portus (harbor, opportunity) — one who has no sense of “harbor,” no self-limiting, pressing on regardless. The KJV uses “importunity” in Luke 11:8 and the adjective is applied traditionally to this widow of Luke 18. Widow from Hebrew almānāh (she who is desolate), Greek chēra (the bereft one). In biblical law, the widow is the paradigm of the unprotected, voiceless, easily-ignored petitioner; the parable's selection of a widow is deliberate.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The parable of the importunate widow (Luke 18:1–8) is introduced by Jesus with explicit interpretive intent: He was telling it “to show that at all times they ought to pray and not to lose heart.” A widow, the biblical icon of social vulnerability, presses an unjust judge — one who neither fears God nor regards man — with repeated petitions for legal protection from an adversary. The judge eventually grants her request not from justice or compassion but from weary self-preservation: “this widow is wearing me out” (the Greek hypopiāzē carries the image of being struck under the eye — a boxing metaphor for relentless battery). Jesus then draws the argument from the lesser to the greater: if an unjust judge grants the widow's request to stop her persistent pleading, how much more will God — who is just, who cares for His elect, and who has bound Himself in covenant to answer — bring about justice for those who cry to Him day and night? The parable's logic is the a fortiori argument: God is infinitely more responsive than the unjust judge; the elect are infinitely more privileged than the powerless widow; therefore persistent prayer before a just and covenant-keeping God is far more warranted than the widow's relentless approach to an unjust man. Jesus closes with an eschatological note (18:8): “When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?” — suggesting that persistent prayer is evidence of living faith, and its absence a symptom of unbelief.

Webster 1828 Definition

The parable of the importunate widow (Luke 18:1–8) teaches persistent, faith-sustained prayer by the a fortiori argument: if an unjust judge yields to a powerless widow's persistence, how much more will the just, covenant-keeping God bring about justice for His elect who cry to Him day and night.

IMPORTUNATE WIDOW, n. The subject of the parable in Luke 18:1–8, introduced by Jesus to teach that disciples “ought to pray at all times and not to lose heart.” A widow — the paradigm of social vulnerability and voicelessness in biblical culture — presses an unjust judge with repeated petition until he grants her request from sheer exhaustion rather than justice.

The parable's logic is a fortiori (from the lesser to the greater): the unjust judge has no care for God or man, yet yields to persistence; God, by contrast, is perfectly just, loves His elect, hears every cry, and is bound by covenant to vindicate them. The gap between the unjust judge and the just God is therefore the measure of why persistent prayer is warranted.

The widow's powerlessness is the parable's deliberate starting point: she has no advocate, no social standing, no legal leverage beyond her persistent presence before the judge. The elect of God are not analogized to the powerful but to the widow — their qualification for answered prayer is not their merit but their persistent faith in the One who can grant what no human judge can.

The Greek hypopiāzē (Luke 18:5, “wearing me out” / “lest she beat me black and blue”) is a boxing metaphor: the widow's persistence is like a fighter's relentless assault under the eye of her opponent. The humor is deliberate — a helpless widow reducing a powerful judge to defensive exhaustion; the point is that persistent petition has power even before unresponsive human authority.

The eschatological close (18:8) — “When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?” — frames persistent prayer as the mark of genuine faith. The parable's lesson is not merely practical (pray longer) but eschatological: the one who prays persistently demonstrates the faith that will endure to the end; the one who loses heart reveals that their trust in God's covenantal faithfulness has faltered.

Key Scripture

Luke 18:1 — "Now He was telling them a parable to show that at all times they ought to pray and not to lose heart, saying,"

Luke 18:3 — "And there was a widow in that city, and she kept coming to him, saying, 'Give me legal protection from my opponent.'"

Luke 18:7 — "now shall not God bring about justice for His elect, who cry to Him day and night — and will He delay long over them?"

Luke 18:8 — "I tell you that He will bring about justice for them speedily. However, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?"

Modern Corruption

Word-faith theology corrupts the parable into a technique for pressuring God into granting whatever is demanded; therapeutic Christianity reduces it to a lesson in self-advocacy; both sever the parable from its eschatological frame and its christological ground in God's covenantal justice.

expand to see more

Word-faith (prosperity-gospel) teaching appropriates the importunate widow as the model for “pressing in” until God releases what one has already “named and claimed.” Kenneth Hagin's “praying through” and Kenneth Copeland's legal-demand theology both invoke the widow as a template for spiritual leverage over God. This inverts the parable entirely: the unjust judge is not God; God is the just Judge who needs no wearing-down. The parable's point is precisely that God is not the unjust judge but infinitely better than him — therefore petition before God is warranted, not because pressure works on Him, but because His covenant reliably does.

Therapeutic pastoral culture detaches the parable from its eschatological close and reduces the lesson to personal persistence in advocating for one's own needs — a model of self-empowerment through vocal self-assertion. This reading strips the parable of its faith-dimension (the widow's persistence is analogized to the elect's persistent faith, not to assertive self-help) and its eschatological weight (“Will the Son of Man find faith on the earth?”). Persistent prayer is not emotional persistence in wanting what one wants; it is faith-sustained persistence in asking what God has promised to give.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The importunate-widow parable draws on the widow's legal vulnerability in Old Testament covenant law (Deuteronomy 24:17; Isaiah 1:17), the Psalter's cry-of-the-oppressed tradition, the prophetic promise of divine vindication for the helpless, and the New Testament's eschatological prayer-context.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 24:17 and Isaiah 1:17 — Israel's covenant law required the defense of widow, orphan, and stranger; the unjust judge who refuses the widow violates these covenant obligations; the parable's setting presupposes a social world where widows' rights were systematically vulnerable.

Psalms of lament (Pss. 10, 22, 35, 88) — the cry-of-the-oppressed tradition in which the righteous sufferer persists in prayer to God despite silence or apparent delay; the widow embodies the anawim's persistent faith.

Luke 11:1–13 (Friend at Midnight / Ask-Seek-Knock) — the parable-and-teaching cluster immediately preceding Luke 18 on persistent prayer; Luke arranges these together to form a theological unit on prayer's persistence and God's responsiveness.

Isaiah 54:4–5 (God as husband of the widow) — God's self-identification as the defender of the widow grounds the parable's eschatological confidence: the elect's advocate is the covenant God who is personally committed to their vindication.

Revelation 6:9–11 (martyrs' cry) — the souls under the altar crying “How long, O Lord?” are the New Testament's most direct parallel to the importunate widow; their persistent eschatological cry is the cry of the whole church awaiting divine justice.

Usage

"The parable's a fortiori logic is its primary pastoral lesson: if a powerless widow's persistence moves an unjust and godless judge, how infinitely more will the persistent prayer of God's elect move the just, covenant-keeping God who has already bound Himself to hear them — the argument should produce prayer, not question it."

"The eschatological close (“When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?”) frames persistent prayer as a mark of genuine faith: the one who stops praying because God seems slow reveals that their trust in His covenantal faithfulness has failed; the one who prays day and night demonstrates that they believe the Judge will act."

"Pastors who address the common complaint “I have been praying for years and nothing has changed” can turn to this parable: it was told precisely for those tempted to lose heart, and its answer is not that God is slow but that the gap between the unjust judge and the just God makes persistent faith in the just God supremely warranted."
